description: Manufacturer's no. 6797. Delivered to MOTAT and reassembled in public view from 31 July 2012. Displayed in the Sir Keith Park Memorial Airfield aviation hall.
The aircraft Cliff Tait flew around the world in 1969. Purchased by the museum in 2006 and repainted in its round-the-world colours.
Was painted in a 1950s RNZAF scheme as the fictitious NZ1708; since repainted in a civil scheme. Acquired from the RNZAF Museum in exchange for genuine Antarctic Auster NZ1707.

Completed 1945 too late for war service; served with the French Aeronavale in East Africa and the South Pacific before acquisition for New Zealand display in 1964. Restored and displayed as a Bomber Command memorial, marked NE181/JN-M on one side and ND752/AA-O on the other.
Manufacturer's no. 3691, built April 1943 as USAAF 42-37208. Imported by NZ Aerial Mapping and flown as Manu Ruuri until withdrawn 31 December 1980. Delivered to MOTAT 1982.

Serial 1865. Donated by Helicopters (NZ) Ltd after over a decade supporting offshore oil rigs and refineries. Recovered as a wreck from Caboolture Queensland in 2007 and restored to flying condition in Brisbane before returning to New Zealand. aviationmuseum.eu records this airframe as a Bell 47G-2 ZK-HGI.
Agricultural topdressing aircraft, suspended from the ceiling of the main aviation display hangar.
Australian-built agricultural aircraft derived from the CAC Wirraway; operated as a New Zealand topdresser 1960-1969.
Composite rebuild based on NZ3039, manufacturer's no. 20218, ex USAAF 41-36385 and RAF EV131.

British construction number 83202 (DHNZ 25); fuselage built at Cowley and shipped to New Zealand, remainder built at Rongotai. Displayed in RNZAF training yellow as NZ775 above the Bomber Command display alongside the Lancaster.
Second MOTAT Tiger Moth, restored and displayed in the main hangar in a civil topdressing configuration. Previously registered ZK-ANN.
Restored to represent ZK-AEK, New Zealand's celebrated Fox Moth; the actual fuselage is that of ZK-APT. The real ZK-AEK is now in Canada as CF-YBM.

Built 1938; flew with Cook Strait Airways as Neptune, impressed by the RNZAF in 1939, later Air Travel (NZ), NAC as Mokai and finally Mount Cook Air Services. Flown to Ardmore in 1974 for preservation.

Built at de Havilland Bankstown as FB.40 A52-19 and converted on the line to trainer A52-1053. Sold to the RNZAF 18 December 1946, delivered to Ohakea April 1947 as NZ2305. Recovered after use as a farm shed.
Manufacturer's no. V1043. Ex-RAF FB.9 used by No. 14 Squadron RNZAF in Singapore, then imported as RNZAF instructional airframe INST171 until 1962.

Manufacturer's no. 14089, BuNo 157909; first flew at Long Beach 11 March 1970 and arrived in Auckland aboard USS Okinawa 17 May 1970. Served with Nos. 75 and 2 Squadrons, stored at Woodbourne from December 2002 and trucked to MOTAT in October 2011.
Built 1945; operated by the RNZAF, Polynesian Airlines and NAC. Under restoration in the workshop hangar.
New Zealand built gyrocopter, originally flown under tow behind a vehicle on an Auckland west coast beach. Suspended from the roof of the display hangar.
All-wood fabric-covered homebuilt from a 1967 design, powered by a modified 1600cc Volkswagen engine. Donated in the 1990s and hung from the ceiling of the main hangar.
The first Fletcher fitted with a turbine engine. Displayed for many years on a plinth at Hamilton Airport before coming to MOTAT.
1930s homebuilt sport biplane; the MOTAT airframe was started at Greenmeadows in Hawke's Bay before the Second World War and sold substantially complete to an owner at Waipukurau in 1948.

Civil registration ZK-CBO. On loan for a period to the Confederate Air Force at Dairy Flat, returned to MOTAT and fully restored for static display in December 2013 with working wing fold and bomb bay.

Nose section, main and rear undercarriage units and all four engines recovered when the complete aircraft could not be moved. Under restoration in the Belfast Hangar; the undercarriage units are a working display.

Ex-RAF K6717, modified by General Aircraft Ltd as a trainer; served with 98(B) Squadron and the Special Duties Flight before assignment to New Zealand on 20 August 1940. Crashed in the hills behind Waikanae 20 November 1941 and later recovered.

Full-scale replica on a plinth at the entrance to the aviation collection, marked P3854/OK-1 to represent the aircraft flown by Sir Keith Park, after whom the MOTAT 2 site is named. It is the second replica, the first having deteriorated in the marine climate.
Complete Electra displayed painted as ZK-AFD. Eight Electras operated in New Zealand, seven for Union Airways and NAC.
Fuselage only, mounted as a cut-away display; displayed for a long period at the MOTAT 1 site.

Manufacturer's no. 4773, built as USAAF 41-38117, transferred to the RAF as FD665 and then to the RNZAF in 1943. The only RNZAF Ventura to survive; recovered from a farm where it lay derelict. Placed in storage with wings removed in 2024 to make room for the Sunderland move.

Manufacturer's no. 2020, oldest of the New Zealand Lodestars. Built as NC25630 for United Airlines, impressed as USAAF 42-53504, to the RAF as AX756, loaned to BOAC as G-AGCN Lake Victoria, later Spanish Air Force, then a New Zealand topdresser for Fieldair from 1957.
Shipped to New Zealand aboard SS Manuel and taken on charge at RNZAF Station Hobsonville 29 October 1941. Recovered after use as a farm shed. Wings removed and placed in storage in 2024.
Flying Flea built in New Zealand in 1936 by E Roy Perkins and Leonard Hawke of Waipukurau with a Douglas Dryad engine.
aliases: Flying Flea; Pou du Ciel; HM14

description: Repainted from wartime camouflage into a civil scheme for display. Known in civil form as the Hawk Trainer 3.

Manufacturer's no. 6322; imported for the Wellington Aero Club and registered 31 July 1947, donated to MOTAT in 1964. Engines removed to reduce weight when it was suspended at MOTAT 1 and remain in storage.

One of the first Harvards delivered to the RNZAF; used as an instructional airframe after retirement from flying. Donated to MOTAT in the museum's first years and now suspended in the main hangar with remotely operable flight controls.
New Zealand light aerobatic biplane built by Fred North at Dannevirke and first flown by Allan McGruer from a field near Whenuapai on 4 January 1934. Rebuilt from major components.
Interpretive replica of Richard Pearse's first flying machine of about 1903.
Second interpretive Pearse replica displayed alongside the first.
Original Pearse relics including his engine and propeller, together with the later Utility Monoplane material.
German-designed training sailplane, suspended in the main display hangar.

Built at Sydenham in 1946 and issued to BOAC as G-AHJR, returned to the RAF April 1948 as SZ584 and handed to the RNZAF 4 September 1953 as NZ4115 'Q for Quebec'. Given to MOTAT 25 February 1967. After fifty years outdoors it was moved into the main aviation display hall and repainted, reported complete in February 2024.
Aranui, manufacturer's no. SH.1559, the world's sole surviving Solent 4. Delivered November 1949 and flown by TEAL on the Coral Route until 1960. Restored from the mid-1980s after years outdoors.
Australian-designed agricultural sesquiplane, fully restored after many years on outdoor display.
Human-powered aircraft begun in February 1966 by Ron Adams in England as a Kremer Prize contender; built of aluminium and balsa under clear plastic film. In storage.
aliases: Adams Ornithopter; Man Powered; ManPowered Aircraft

description: Corporal E tactical ballistic missile on long-term loan from the Smithsonian Institution, displayed horizontally beside the main science building at the Great North Road site.
